ABID Panel Practice

Twenty questions. Two panels. A mix of foundational skills, laboratory decisions, and advanced investigations.

Instructions and panel conventions

ABID Panel Practice

Work through 20 original questions using two antibody identification (ABID) panels. Foundation questions build panel-reading skills. Application questions connect results to laboratory decisions. Advanced questions combine several findings or testing methods.

Ungraded practice: There is no time limit, and you may repeat the quiz. The first-try count is for self-assessment only, not a grade or a prediction of certification-exam performance. Use Check answer to see immediate feedback, then retry or continue. The first-try counter is for your own review.

How to use the panels: Open a panel at full size or use its text version. Unless a question says otherwise, AHG results are from a tube indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) using anti-IgG after incubation at 37°C. In the CC column, √ indicates that added IgG-coated check cells reacted; NT means not tested. A 0 in an antigen column means antigen-negative; a 0 in AHG means nonreactive.

Case boundaries: These supplied teaching panels are not verified commercial lot profiles and include unusual antigen combinations. Use the displayed values for the exercises; do not treat them as typical donor phenotypes or silently correct them. Any new patient history or additional test result appears explicitly in the question and applies only to that question. Do not assume unprovided DAT, autocontrol, or patient typing results. Where an exclusion or confirmation rule is specified, use that rule for the exercise.

Use only the information for the current question. Added scenarios are independent unless a question explicitly links them. When a later sample or different method is described, the image remains the original reference panel.

Choose one best answer. Use the thinking prompt when useful, then review the explanation and try again. These are independently written practice questions, not actual or endorsed ASCP examination items, and they do not cover the entire SBB exam.

Terms used in the questions

IAT: Indirect antiglobulin test, used here to detect antibodies reacting with test red cells. DAT: Direct antiglobulin test, used to detect antibody or complement already attached to red cells. Autocontrol: The patient's plasma tested against red cells from the patient's sample.

Adsorption: Removing antibodies from plasma by allowing them to bind to selected red cells. Eluate: Antibody recovered from red cells for further testing. Allogeneic adsorption: Adsorption using donor cells rather than the patient's own cells.

Phenotype: The antigens expressed on red cells. Genotyping: DNA testing used to help predict antigen expression. Mixed-field: A mixture of reacting and nonreacting red cells. Fy(a+b−): Fyᵃ is present and Fyᵇ is absent; Kidd notation works the same way.
